chapters.1: John opens by introducing Jesus as the eternal 'Word' who was with God and became flesh, bringing light and truth into the world. John the Baptist testifies that he is not the Christ but points to Jesus as the Lamb of God. Jesus then calls his first disciples, including Andrew, Peter, Philip, and Nathanael, who begin to recognize him as the Messiah and Son of God.
chapters.2: Jesus performs his first miracle, turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana at his mother's request. He then travels to Jerusalem for Passover and drives merchants and money-changers out of the temple, declaring it should not be a marketplace. When asked for a sign of his authority, he speaks cryptically of raising a destroyed 'temple' in three days, a statement later understood to refer to his own body and resurrection.
chapters.3: Nicodemus, a Jewish religious leader, comes to Jesus at night, and Jesus tells him that a person must be 'born again' by the Spirit to enter God's kingdom. Jesus explains that God sent his Son not to condemn the world but to save it, in the well-known statement that God loved the world enough to give his only Son. John the Baptist's disciples report that people are now following Jesus, and John responds that he rejoices to see Jesus increase while his own role decreases.
chapters.4: Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well and offers her 'living water,' revealing that he knows her past and that true worship is a matter of spirit and truth rather than location. She recognizes him as the Messiah and tells her townspeople, many of whom come to believe in him. Jesus then returns to Galilee and heals a Roman official's dying son from a distance simply by speaking the word.
chapters.5: Jesus heals a man who had been disabled for thirty-eight years at the pool of Bethesda, healing him on the Sabbath, which angers the religious leaders. When they confront him, Jesus explains that he acts in unity with his Father and that the Father has given him authority to give life and to judge. He points to the testimony of John the Baptist, his own miraculous works, and the Scriptures themselves as evidence that he was sent by God.
chapters.6: Jesus feeds five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, and later walks on water to reach his disciples during a storm on the lake. He then teaches that he is the 'bread of life' sent from heaven, explaining that true life comes from believing in him, a hard teaching that causes many followers to leave him. Peter, however, affirms that the twelve disciples will stay, since Jesus alone has the words of eternal life.
chapters.7: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles despite his brothers' skepticism and teaches openly in the temple, causing division among the people over whether he is the Christ. He offers 'rivers of living water' to anyone who comes to him thirsty, a promise referring to the Holy Spirit. The religious leaders try to arrest him but hesitate, while even some of their own officers are struck by the authority of his words.
chapters.8: Jesus shows mercy to a woman caught in adultery, telling her accusers that whoever is without sin may cast the first stone, and then tells her to go and sin no more. He declares himself the 'light of the world' and engages in intense debate with religious leaders about his identity and authority, teaching that the truth will set people free. The chapter ends with Jesus making the startling claim 'before Abraham was, I am,' prompting an attempt to stone him.
chapters.9: Jesus heals a man who was born blind by making clay with his own saliva and having him wash in the pool of Siloam, restoring his sight. The religious leaders interrogate the healed man and his parents, refusing to believe the miracle came from God and ultimately expelling the man from the synagogue. Jesus finds him afterward, reveals himself as the Son of God, and contrasts true spiritual sight with the willful blindness of his critics.
chapters.10: Jesus describes himself as the Good Shepherd who knows his sheep personally and lays down his life for them, unlike a hired hand who abandons the flock in danger. He declares that he and the Father are one, which provokes some to accuse him of blasphemy and attempt to stone him. He escapes and withdraws across the Jordan, where many people come to believe in him.
chapters.11: Jesus' friend Lazarus dies, and when Jesus arrives in Bethany four days later, he weeps with Lazarus's grieving sisters, Mary and Martha. He then calls Lazarus out of the tomb, raising him back to life, a miracle that leads many to believe but also pushes the religious leaders to begin plotting Jesus' death. The high priest Caiaphas reasons that it would be better for one man to die than for the whole nation to suffer.
chapters.12: Mary anoints Jesus' feet with expensive perfume at a dinner in Bethany, an act Jesus says anticipates his burial, while Judas objects. Jesus then rides into Jerusalem to a crowd's enthusiastic welcome, and he speaks about his coming death using the image of a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit. Despite many signs, most of the people still do not believe, fulfilling an old prophecy about spiritual blindness.
chapters.13: At the Last Supper, Jesus washes his disciples' feet as an example of humble service, teaching them to do the same for one another. He predicts that Judas will betray him and that Peter will deny him three times before the night is over, though he also gives the disciples a new commandment to love one another as he has loved them.
chapters.14: Jesus comforts his troubled disciples, promising to prepare a place for them in his Father's house and declaring himself 'the way, the truth, and the life.' He promises to send the Holy Spirit, called the Comforter, to teach and guide them after he is gone, and he leaves them with a gift of peace unlike anything the world can give.
chapters.15: Jesus describes himself as the true vine and his followers as branches, teaching that fruitful living depends on staying closely connected to him. He gives the command to love one another as he has loved them, even to the point of laying down one's life, and warns that the world will hate his followers just as it hated him.
chapters.16: Jesus warns his disciples of coming persecution but promises that the Holy Spirit will come to guide them into truth and to convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment. He speaks of their coming sorrow turning to joy, comparing it to the pain of childbirth followed by joy, and assures them that despite coming hardship, he has already overcome the world.
chapters.17: Jesus prays to the Father before his arrest, asking to be glorified and reflecting on the eternal life he has given his followers through knowing God. He prays specifically for his disciples' protection and unity, and extends that prayer to all future believers, asking that they would be one just as he and the Father are one.
chapters.18: Jesus is betrayed by Judas and arrested in the garden of Gethsemane, where Peter cuts off a servant's ear before Jesus heals him and submits to arrest. Jesus is brought before the high priest and questioned, while Peter denies knowing him three times as predicted. Pilate, the Roman governor, examines Jesus and finds no basis for a charge, but the crowd demands the release of the criminal Barabbas instead.
chapters.19: Pilate has Jesus flogged and mocked by soldiers before reluctantly giving in to the crowd's demand for crucifixion. Jesus is crucified between two criminals, entrusts his mother to the care of his beloved disciple, and dies after declaring 'It is finished.' Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus take his body and bury it in a nearby tomb.
chapters.20: Mary Magdalene finds Jesus' tomb empty and runs to tell Peter and another disciple, who confirm it but don't yet understand. Jesus then appears to Mary, and later to the gathered disciples, breathing peace on them and giving them the Holy Spirit. A week later he appears again to convince the doubting disciple Thomas, who touches his wounds and declares him 'my Lord and my God.'
chapters.21: The risen Jesus appears to his disciples by the Sea of Galilee, helping them catch a huge number of fish after a fruitless night, and shares a breakfast of bread and fish with them on the shore. He then restores Peter through a threefold exchange about love, commissioning him to 'feed my sheep' and hinting at the death Peter would eventually face. The book closes by affirming that this account is the trustworthy testimony of the disciple whom Jesus loved.
